summary: A dense, dial-turning euro where every turn you're juggling which of the sun/shadow/dark zones are active, what your dice-based turn order will be, and which of several long-term engines (temple building, obelisk tiles, gods' favor) to advance. It rewards careful sequencing and planning several rounds ahead more than reacting to opponents.
praised: The rotating obelisk shadow mechanic that constantly reshuffles which actions are available
Dice-driven turn order as a genuinely interesting risk/planning layer rather than pure luck
Deep, interlocking systems that reward long-term planning and give strong replayability via variable setup
Satisfying sense of building an efficient engine across the temple/obelisk/gods tracks
criticised: Steep rules overhead and long teach for a game that plays fairly abstractly once learned
Turn order dice can feel swingy or unfair to players who dislike variance affecting planning
Significant analysis paralysis, especially in the middle game with many viable lines
Egyptian theme feels pasted on top of what is a very mechanical, abstract euro

interaction.kind: action-space blocking and turn-order jockeying, otherwise mostly parallel engine-building

scoring.why: points accumulate across several parallel systems (temple tiles, obelisk pattern-building, gods' favor tracks) so the winner is usually whoever balances multiple engines rather than maxing one
